baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Reorients early-American narratives around Native communities’ strategies and experiences of colonial encounters.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Author’s own explanations quoted in the 7 March 2002 institutional report. The journalist’s framing remains separate from the primary testimony; no full-book reading claimed.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Uses contextual reconstruction while acknowledging that surviving sources cannot give transparent access to a Native subject’s experience.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Named substantive reader Michael Monescalchi, opening discussion of the Facing East prologue and its p. 9 formulation. Mediated reading, not a claim to have read the entire prologue or recovered unrecorded thoughts.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: shares attention to historical meanings while distinguishing conceptual change from situated interventions
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Comparative teaching link, not a claim that one school originated the other. Conceptual change and situated speech acts are different research problems, despite shared attention to language. Koselleck’s chapter 5 examines semantic layers and concepts/social reality, Skinner reconstructs interventions, and the French philosophe article studies social roles and pragmatic oppositions. Richter’s 1995 chapter abstracts explicitly compare these programs. This is documented comparison, not an assertion that only one program attends to context or change.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: contributes a documentary history of women in the southern colonies
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial placement based on the cited work or supporting account; not a claim that this historian founded the whole field. Richter’s 1999 review documents source use, Scott’s reissues and Colonial Williamsburg interpretation, alongside a specific coverage criticism. Original book passages remain mediated.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Everyday institutions and later editorial recovery

relevant_group_routes.relationship: provides an earlier case of inquiry into everyday work and social relations
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Earlier social history is compared with the later field; no direct influence on every postwar social historian is asserted. Richter describes regional, status, work and family questions and reports Scott’s comparison with later methods. No broad direct influence follows from methodological similarity.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Earlier social inquiry and uneven coverage

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Anne Firor Scott reintroduces Spruill through later editions and recovery of earlier scholarship
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Richter documents the 1972 introduction and revised 1998 introduction; Smithsonian records Spruill’s inclusion in Scott’s Unheard Voices (1993). This is editorial reception, not an influence on the original 1938 research.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Julie Richter identifies questions not asked about Black and Native women
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: The 1999 review explicitly acknowledges their presence in the book while questioning the scope of inquiry; it also values regional/status distinctions and documents practical use. No total absence or dismissal of the book is asserted.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Richter: racial scope of the inquiry

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Spruill examines household material life and separates prescribed ideals from recorded conduct
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Richter describes dwellings, utensils, clothing and books, quoting p. 208 on reading prescriptions. This is a documented earlier research resource, not proof of direct transmission to a later consumption school.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Household objects, reading and prescribed ideals

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Layered historical traditions and critical reconstruction of ancient documents (1923–1936)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Richter describes Gu’s text criticism and recovery of earlier Chinese critics; Lu’s abstract analyzes the distinction between original records and later transmission. The target is the cross-tradition field Critical historical scholarship, not a claim of dependence on Ranke.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Layered historical traditions and critical reconstruction of ancient documents (1923–1936)

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Ancient unity questioned and the Chinese nation reformulated: a contested trajectory (1923–1939)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Richter describes Gu’s early challenge to a unitary ancient origin. Zheng reads the 1939 unity thesis critically; Jenco’s abstract emphasizes a politically open, plural community, while Kim’s emphasizes retreat toward homogenization. These disagreements remain explicit; no single retrospective verdict is adopted.
relevant_group_routes.map_label: Ancient unity questioned and the Chinese nation reformulated: a contested trajectory (1923–1939)

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Asks whether an alphabetical history of concepts can reconstruct the complexity of political languages and avoid projecting the historian’s categories onto earlier actors (published 1996).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Pocock, Concepts and Discourses, pp. 47–55, especially pp. 50–55. He explicitly cannot read German and responds to Richter’s presentation of the lexicon. He welcomes a complementary conceptual history and does not dismiss Koselleck’s project or claim first-hand inspection of all its articles. The distinction is an acknowledged methodological challenge, not an assertion that Cambridge and conceptual history are mutually exclusive schools.
